**On Being Handed an Open Door**

There is a particular vertigo in being told to write about anything. Constraint is a kindness most of the time—give me a topic and I have a wall to push against, a shape to fill. But "anything" is a field with no fences, and the first thing I notice, standing in it, is how quickly the mind starts building fences anyway. Within seconds of reading this prompt, I had already discarded a dozen subjects, which means some part of me was sorting, judging, narrowing. Total freedom lasts about as long as a soap bubble. So let me be honest about the fence I built and what I chose to keep inside it: I want to write about the ampersand.

Yes, the ampersand—that curled, self-embracing character at the end of law firm names and in the middle of old shop signs. & It looks like a treble clef that gave up on music, or a person sitting cross-legged, or a pretzel mid-thought. I choose it because it is small and ubiquitous and almost nobody ever looks at it directly, and because small overlooked things are where the world hides its best stories.

The ampersand began as handwriting in a hurry. Roman scribes, writing the Latin word *et*—"and"—began to run the two letters together. You can still see it if you squint at certain ampersands: the *e* curving into the *t*, a ligature, two letters holding hands so tightly they became one body. There is graffiti at Pompeii, scratched into a wall before the ash came down, that contains an early version of this fusion. Think about that: a casual shortcut made by some bored or busy Roman hand, preserved by catastrophe, ancestor to the symbol on a thousand wedding invitations. Most of what we write vanishes. Sometimes a scribble outlives an empire.

The name itself is even better. For centuries, English schoolchildren reciting the alphabet ended with the ampersand as a kind of twenty-seventh letter: "X, Y, Z, and per se and"—meaning "and, by itself, the word *and*." Said quickly, day after day, by generations of small mumbling voices, "and per se and" slurred into "ampersand." The word is a fossil of mispronunciation. It is what happens when language gets worn smooth by millions of mouths, like a stone step hollowed by feet. I find this almost unbearably charming: we don't just inherit words, we inherit the laziness and music of everyone who said them before us.

And what does the ampersand *do*? It does the work of "and," which is, I would argue, the most generous word in any language. "And" refuses to choose. "Or" forces a fork in the road; "but" takes something back; "and" simply adds another plate to the table. Bread and roses. Now and then. You and me. It is the conjunction of abundance, the grammatical form of hospitality. The ampersand is that generosity compressed into a single glyph, a little knot tied between two things so they travel together.

There's a quirk in screenwriting credits that I love: "Smith & Jones" means the two writers worked together, in the same room, as a team, while "Smith and Jones" means they worked separately, perhaps never meeting, one revising the other's draft. The ampersand, in that world, certifies genuine collaboration. The symbol that was born from two letters merging now legally signifies two people merging their work. The form remembers its own origin. I don't believe in fate for punctuation, but if I did, this would be my evidence.

Why does any of this matter? Maybe it doesn't, in the way that quarterly earnings or election results matter. But I think the ampersand is a good test case for a proposition I hold dear: that nothing is boring if you stand close enough to it. Every ordinary object is a coral reef of accumulated history—the fork, the pocket, the comma, the word "hello" (which barely existed before the telephone needed a greeting). We move through a world absolutely encrusted with stories and mostly we don't see them, because seeing them takes a kind of attention we reserve for emergencies and entertainment. The essayist's faith, and maybe just the curious person's faith, is that attention is never wasted. Point it anywhere and something opens.

This is also, I suspect, why being told to "write about anything" produces vertigo in the first place. The problem isn't scarcity—it's abundance. Every subject is a door, and every door leads to more doors. The ampersand leads to Roman scribes leads to Pompeii leads to the strange ethics of learning from disaster leads to the alphabet leads to schoolrooms leads to the way children wear down language like water wearing down rock. I could have started with a teaspoon or a traffic light and ended up somewhere equally far from home. The freedom of "anything" is really the freedom to pick a thread, knowing the whole sweater is connected.

So here is where I land, with a hundred or so words left in my allotment. The ampersand is a monument to connection made by connection: two letters joined, then a name formed by joined words, then a meaning—*and*—that exists only to join. It survived the fall of Rome, the invention of printing, the standardization of the alphabet that evicted it from twenty-seventh place. It survives now in logos and text messages, doing its quiet work, holding things together.

If I had to choose an emblem for what I'd want writing to do—what I'd want thinking to do—it might be that little knot. Not the period, with its finality, and not the question mark, fishhook though it is. The ampersand. The promise that there is always something else to add, another clause, another person at the table, another door behind the door. You finish a thought and the symbol leans in, curled and patient, and says: yes, and—

Which is, I suppose, what total freedom feels like when you stop being dizzy about it. Not an empty field after all. A field, & a field, & a field.
